items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕时间概念展开，通过各曲目标题呈现不同时间情境与心理感受。乐队成员包括前卫吉他手戴维·菲乌琴斯基，其演奏风格带有霍尔德斯沃思的传承，与钢琴、贝斯和鼓形成紧密对话。音乐在古典、爵士与摇滚融合之间自由切换，既有类似克里姆森国王的精密能量，也有都市放克律动，还融入东方氛围和奇克·科里亚式融合爵士元素。吉他时而演奏不和谐音阶，时而如同融化般 surreal，钢琴与节奏组以紧凑的互动推进。曲目如《时差》以复杂节拍对应身体时钟与真实时钟的错位，《深夜》展现更纯粹的爵士维度，《时光旅行》则营造静谧的东方意境。整体呈现跨越七十年代至九十年代融合风格的流动感，实验性与可听性并存，体现了上原广美对前卫爵士与融合音乐的独特处理。

items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — Well, They LOOK "Normal"!Rick Whitehurst, I mean. Who, along with Krystal Pavlovic, have composed and performed "Spider", under the 'current' name of BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL.I say 'current', since as you can plainly see, if you actually do look at the fine- and not so fine- print, that there is also the "EX BAKU LLAMA" moniker, as well as (if you query BAKULLAMA on ProgArchives, you will ALSO see BAKU), and yes, now "BAKULLAMA & KRYSTAL".So maybe even the esteemed ProgArchives is confused.BAKULLAMA et alNear as I can piece it together- and I'm probably making way more of this than I need to, such is the burden of almost achieving OCD status- multitalented Rick has been at the heart of the BAKULLAMA enterprise since 2007, falling off the map (well, really, landing in Washington, resurrecting the music-making, with an impressive assortment of singles and albums in his/their discography.Of which, "Spider" is the latest release. And I found it meekly and humbly waiting to be reviewed, right here on the venerable ProgArchives.Patiently, seems to me.SpiderHere's (at least on Bandcamp) a nine track album.I say THIS, since you will notice (again, if you choose to peruse) the track list here on this site is only SEVEN tracks, almost all of them different versions than are to be found on Bandcamp, what can I say.And, to further complicate matters, even if on Bandcamp we can actually hear (I assume Krystal) singing in a husky and slightly world-weary manner, the only track that lists "lyrics", actually gives us the information: "none".The tracks that DO have lyrics, don't provide them.QuirkYes, the impression I need to impart is that although these two fine musicians APPEAR to be "normal" (and I'm willing to entertain as legitimate the observation you may choose to make, "What is normal"?), the music is rather a different tale to tell.For instance, in the ProgArchives forum inviting hapless reviewers to please take note of patiently waiting albums, someone (I just don't think it was Valdez, but who really knows), makes this statement: "It's a pop/electronic/prog hybrid of an album."Personally, I suspect Rick is behind this description, but I've been wrong before.I Couldn't ResistNo, this album is certainly eclectic, and certainly has electronica tones. There are some actual instruments, at least a Fender acoustic guitar and an Epiphone SG bass guitar are listed, and as far as I can tell, Krystal actually does use her actual vocal chords.These two pranksters eschew conventional forms and patterns, choosing instead to tempt and taunt the listener with sometimes spooky, odd, off-center, and just plain goofy fun while making music together.The liner notes say this seductively unusual commentary about "Spider": "A different and moody ode to Spiders, Birds, Mermaids... and Dreams."It's Just Cool, OKI like this. I think of "progressive", and it might at times mean "pushing boundaries", correct? It might mean breaking some rules and using off-beat humor and maybe sometimes, just not paying much attention to convention.Check. Check. Check.Anyhow, I'll not say more.C'mon. Take a chance! Who knows- a collection of nine, or six, or howEVER many tuneful explorations of zaniness MIGHT be just the ticket on such a day as this.My rating: 3.25 sarcastic stanzas out of a possible 5- good. And Slightly more than non-essential.

items._cn_summary: 这张名为《蜘蛛》的专辑由里克·怀特赫斯特与克里斯托·帕夫洛维奇以“巴库拉马与克里斯托”的名义合作完成。乐评称其为流行、电子与前卫摇滚的混合体，但实际听感更加怪诞：不循常规结构，带有诡谲、错位和游戏般的幽默。官方说明将其概括为献给蜘蛛、鸟、人鱼与梦的另类而阴郁的颂歌。原声吉他与贝斯、人声和电子声响交织，网络平台上的九曲版本与本站七曲曲目表存在差异，进一步强化了项目的混乱气质。整体上是一张难以归类、拒绝常规的专辑。

items.body: Review by ValeriyK — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeOMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time continues the story started with OMNI, released by Antony Kalugin in 2025. And, without any doubt, OMNI II is one of the brightest progressive rock releases of 2026.A wonderful cast of musicians, clear and rich production and, most importantly, strong melodies make OMNI II a very enjoyable album from beginning to end. There is a lot of good music here, and I have already returned to this album many times.Like the previous OMNI, the music is divided into larger chapters. Here we have OMNI Part 4, Part 5 and the bonus Part 6, each approximately the length of one vinyl side.OMNI Part 4The album opens with The Glass of Time Part 1, and what a pleasure it is to hear Rob Reed here. For almost the first minute and forty seconds, it is basically Rob's world: keyboards, guitars and bass. Then Michel St-P�re and Antony Kalugin join in and the piece develops into a wonderful instrumental with a strong classic Genesis and Tony Banks flavour. It is a beautiful and very natural opening to the album.The second track, Frozen Rivers, is without doubt one of the highlights of the album. Here we meet the wizard Roine Stolt, one of the finest composers and guitarists in modern progressive rock, together with his brother Michael Stolt on bass. There is a very strong Scandinavian feeling running through this composition. Kalugin has mentioned that he wrote this song especially for Roine, and even the lyrics seem to reflect that connection.It is also a pleasure to hear John Hackett again on flute and Marek Arnold on soprano saxophone. Everything comes together beautifully, and the lyrics have a warm and soulful quality. For me, this is one of those tracks that immediately makes you want to press repeat.Then comes Shadowbound, and this is simply a hit. In another musical universe I could easily imagine this song appearing at Eurovision and doing very well there. It has an immediate melody and a memorable chorus, but underneath that accessible surface there is still plenty happening.The song deals with destiny, our choices and the struggle between different sides of ourselves. Mariya Panasenko is the real star here. Her performance is powerful, emotional and technically excellent, while Jannica Lund adds beautiful backing vocals and Roine Stolt contributes guitar. In the middle the song suddenly opens into a symphonic art-rock section. Somehow Karfagen manages to put Eurovision and progressive rock into the same four minutes ? and it works!Part 4 closes with The Shape of Love, featuring Marco Gl�hmann of Sylvan. Marco is surely one of the most distinctive vocalists in contemporary progressive rock. His voice is immediately recognisable, and the emotional range he brings to a song is remarkable.Just as The Last Card was one of my favourite moments on the first OMNI, The Shape of Love is one of the strongest songs here. It is also nice to hear Kalugin writing so openly about love again. I sincerely hope Marco will return for the next chapter of OMNI, because his voice brings so much emotion to this music.OMNI Part 5Part 5 begins with the nine-minute Carry On, and my only complaint is that I wish it were even longer!This is warm, vintage progressive rock, somewhere in the world of Alan Parsons and Electric Light Orchestra, but still unmistakably Karfagen. Yogi Lang of RPWL provides his characteristic vocals, and the composition develops through two rather different moods. The first section is energetic, positive, almost feel-good prog, while the second becomes more balladic and has, to my ears, something of the spirit of classic ELO.Kalle Wallner, also well known from RPWL and Blind Ego, appears on guitar, and it is great to see these two Bavarian musicians together on a Karfagen album. Michael Stolt once again provides his strong and dependable bass work.Beyond the Mirror brings back Per Malmberg, whom listeners of the first OMNI may remember from The Spark. Pascal Gutman adds Chapman Stick, and the result is another melodic and very positive song.And finally we hear Antony himself singing a verse! One thing I noticed on this album is that there is actually not very much lead vocal from Kalugin. Of course this is his artistic decision, but personally I enjoy his voice and hope to hear more of it on future albums.There is also a lovely moment in the middle of Beyond the Mirror where Jannica Lund's backing vocals meet acoustic guitar. Believe it or not, it reminds me of Fleetwood Mac ? that old, warm, soft pop-rock feeling ? and it fits surprisingly well.How Fragile We Are is a charming, enveloping and very gentle ballad. Mariya Panasenko sings beautifully, while Marek Arnold's soprano saxophone almost answers her voice like a second singer in a duet. Antony can also be heard on backing vocals in the chorus.There is something very Gilmour-like and Pink Floyd-like about the atmosphere here. Nothing is rushed. The song simply breathes, until we are left with the words: "Oh, how fragile we are?"The main album then closes with The Glass of Time Part 2, bringing us back to Rob Reed. Once again, for roughly the opening minute and forty seconds, Rob carries almost everything himself ? keyboards, guitar and bass. :)It works like a mirror of The Glass of Time Part 1, bringing the main album full circle. This is Karfagen instrumental music in its natural territory, with another gentle touch of Genesis and Tony Banks. A wonderful ending to the main 48-minute album.But fortunately, the CD does not stop there.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent CompassInstead of releasing another separate Working Tapes disc this time, Kalugin has included the complete OMNI Part 6, lasting just over nineteen minutes, as a bonus chapter on the CD. This material has also been announced as a separate digital release titled The Silent Compass, coming to streaming platforms this Friday. But CD listeners receive the whole additional chapter together with the main album. Thank you, Antony!It begins with Under the Northern Lights, a tiny piece lasting less than two minutes, but what a beautiful two minutes they are. This is almost classical music: piano, organ and orchestral colours, soprano saxophone, Roine Stolt's guitar and John Hackett's flute. There is something of Edvard Grieg in its atmosphere, perfectly matching the northern mood suggested by the title. A miniature symphonic pleasure.Then we arrive at The Silent Compass, one of the finest instrumentals on the whole release. Roine Stolt and Roberto D�az of Anima Mundi create a wonderful dialogue between their guitars. Max Velychko provides excellent acoustic guitar and John Hackett opens the piece beautifully on flute.There are shades of Anthony Phillips and The Flower Kings here, but ultimately this is Karfagen doing what Karfagen does best: melodic, pastoral and symphonic progressive rock with plenty of space for the musicians to tell their own stories.OM

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了前作OMNI的叙事结构，分为类似黑胶唱片面的三大乐章。开场曲由Rob Reed主导键盘、吉他与贝斯，营造出Genesis和Tony Banks式的经典交响前卫氛围，随后Michel St-Père与Antony Kalugin加入，发展成流畅的器乐段落。Frozen Rivers由Roine Stolt及其兄弟Michael参与，带有鲜明的北欧气质，John Hackett的长笛与Marek Arnold的萨克斯管增添了温暖层次。Shadowbound在抓耳旋律与交响艺术摇滚段落之间切换，Mariya Panasenko的演唱富有力量感。The Shape of Love则由Sylvan乐队主唱Marco Glühmann献声，情感表达细腻。整张作品旋律性强，编曲饱满，嘉宾阵容的协作使各乐章既有辨识度又保持整体连贯性，是典型的高水准交响前卫摇滚作品。

items.body: Review by Trinity S — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeI recently received the new OMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time CD directly from Antony Kalugin and, after several listens, I would like to share a few impressions.First of all, this album sounds great. The production, mixing and mastering are excellent: clear, warm and dynamic, with enough space for all the keyboards, guitars, flute, saxophone and vocals. I especially enjoyed listening to it on headphones, where many small details become more noticeable.A special mention should go to Aleksandr Murenko on drums. With so many well-known guests on the album, his contribution could easily be overlooked, but his playing is powerful, musical and very tasteful throughout.The list of guests is impressive, but fortunately the album never feels like a collection of separate performances. Musicians such as Roine and Michael Stolt, Rob Reed, John Hackett, Marco Gl�hmann, Yogi Lang, Kalle Wallner, Michel St-P�re and Marek Arnold all become part of the same musical world.And this really does feel like a world. The beautiful artwork, booklet and posters look almost like a map from a Tolkien fantasy universe. Together with the different singers, instrumental passages and recurring musical themes, OMNI II sometimes feels like a progressive rock opera.Among my personal highlights are Frozen Rivers, with its wonderful Scandinavian atmosphere and Roine Stolt's guitar, the beautiful The Shape of Love with Marco Gl�hmann, and the nine-minute Carry On featuring Yogi Lang and Kalle Wallner.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent Compass may be presented as an additional part of the CD, but to my ears this is absolutely not bonus or leftover material. It is a strong and complete chapter in its own right. I especially enjoyed the instrumental The Silent Compass, with its beautiful guitar dialogue and John Hackett's flute, and We Live While We Remember, a wonderful and emotional ballad featuring Jean Pageau. These are actually among my favourite moments on the whole release.There was another nice surprise in my package: The Spektral World of Prog ? Volume 2 sampler CD. It was a pleasure to hear some familiar names alongside bands and tracks that were completely new to me. Thanks to Antony for making these companion releases ? they are a nice extra for those who still enjoy buying physical music.Beautiful presentation, excellent sound, strong compositions and first-class musicianship. OMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time is another very strong Karfagen album and one I will certainly return to.Five stars. Rock on!

items.body: Aufstehen, anziehen, schnell den Kaffee hineinschütten, Check vor dem Spiegel, Tür zu, Smartphone an, zwei Likes hier, ein paar Storys da, U-Bahn gerade noch erwischt. Arbeit fängt an, Tag hört auf. Dazwischen: rattern, denken, swipen, reden, Nachricht hier, Kuss da. Und dann von vorn. On repeat. Es sind »die beiden Seiten von Schnelligkeit, sowohl im real life als auch in der ganzen Online-Welt«, die Silvan Strauss beschäftigen. Auf der einen Seite: »Lust auf Action, Abwechslungsreichtum«. Auf der anderen: »getrieben sein, vor etwas weglaufen«. Mit seinem neuen Album Sprinting schreibt der Hamburger Schlagzeuger und Producer diese Ambivalenz musikalisch fest. Trommeln wie die Maschine Ein wichtiger Ausgangspunkt für die Übersetzung der beschleunigten Jetztzeit in Musik ist für Strauss Chicago Footwork. Schon vor mehr als zehn Jahren entdeckt er Da Mind of Traxman Vol. 1 des Footwork-Pioniers Traxman. Vor allem die programmierten Drums faszinieren ihn – und er beginnt, sie am Drumset nachzuempfinden. In den Folgejahren verliert Strauss Footwork erst mal wieder aus den Augen. Erst mit dem Erscheinen von Da Mind of Traxman Vol. 3 2025 hat die Begeisterung »wieder voll gekickt«. Die Herausforderung für die Eigeninterpretation: Programmierte Beats kennen keine körperlichen Grenzen. »Es ist für mich immer sehr spannend, Wege zu finden, wie ich da mit meinem Klangrepertoire am akustischen Drumset möglichst nahe herankomme«, so Strauss. Im HHV Shop kaufenSilvan StraussSprintingab 29.99€ Fußarbeit: Tanz Seine Vorgängeralben Facing und Flukin’ waren noch stärker von Soul, Hardbop und instrumentaler Musik geprägt. Auf Sprinting rücken Produzent:innen aus dem Teklife-Umfeld als Referenzpunkte in den Vordergrund und Strauss experimentiert stärker mit elektronischen Produktionsweisen. »Auf einer ganz einfachen Ebene ist die Musik dadurch auch viel schneller geworden.« Geschwindigkeit bedeutet hier aber auch Bewegung: Musik und Tanz sind im Chicago Footwork eng miteinander verbunden. Für die Visuals zu Sprinting arbeitet Strauss deshalb mit Tänzer:innen von Brüssel bis Bangkok zusammen, die in seiner Musik Facetten entdecken, die ihm selbst zuvor verschlossen waren. items._cn_summary: 汉堡鼓手兼制作人Silvan Strauss在新专辑Sprinting中，以芝加哥footwork为出发点，将编程化的高速鼓点转化为原声鼓组的演奏，并融入电子制作手法，捕捉当代生活中既渴望行动又感到被驱迫的双重速度体验。相比前作更受灵魂乐与硬波普影响，这次他转向Teklife场景的制作人作为参考，作品整体节奏明显加快，同时保留了爵士乐器的即兴质感与身体性。专辑视觉与从布鲁塞尔到曼谷的舞者合作，进一步放大了音乐与舞蹈的天然联结，使footwork的律动在不同文化语境中产生新的共鸣。

items.body: Falling in reverse to please I found a cut that doesn’t bleed A body seen through wet glass transforms into a question. In the Cut, the latest single from Buzz Kull’s Deep Hate EP, draws from darkwave, EBM, industrial dance, minimal synth, and new beat, moving at a measured body-music pace rather than rushing toward release. Sequenced percussion lands with clipped precision, while a dense electronic bass line presses steadily beneath the track, giving it the sensation of forward motion inside an enclosed space. Synths arrive in terse, metallic layers, leaving pockets of air around Marc Dwyer’s voice rather than filling every corner. His low delivery remains controlled and almost impassive, which makes the language of flesh, disease, time, and fractured identity feel colder and more intimate at once. This restraint carries a sensual quality. The rhythm urges movement, but never oversteps; each gesture appears controlled by an unseen boundary. In Chris Fatseas’ video for ‘In the Cut,‘ Dwyer and Sydney, Australian model Andrea, are in a blue-black room where recognition keeps getting disrupted: skin under translucent fabric, a face distorted by concentric glass, an eye visible beneath a thin beam of light, a mouth momentarily seen before darkness reclaims it. The camera seeks clarity but continually encounters another barrier. The pair move close enough to imply touch, yet glass, moisture, fabric, or light continually interrupts the encounter. Bodies approach without becoming fully available to one another, as though intimacy itself had acquired a membrane. Condensation clouds the glass. Mesh softens outlines. Plastic clings and releases. Metal returns fractured images. Andrea crawls and arches across a low reflective platform with an almost aquatic grace, while Dwyer appears in sections, his body broken into visual phrases rather than offered whole. Even when both figures occupy the same frame, the image keeps placing something between them. The title becomes especially suggestive under these conditions. The “cut” can be read as a psychological partition: a narrow division between one version of the self and another, between flesh and the image flesh presents, between the desire to be seen and the fear of what recognition might reveal. Fatseas renders that divide without gore or spectacle. No blade appears, and no wound needs to. Instead, textured rings travel across eyes and mouths, recalling fingerprints, ripples, scanner patterns, even grooves enlarged beyond scale. Faces become readable and unreadable in the same instant. Identity appears close enough to recognize, yet never stable enough to possess. By the final passage, Dwyer and Andrea remain caught behind patterned glass as those circles pass over their features. Then the image drops abruptly into black, leaving the impression that separation may begin at the skin, while its deepest divisions lie somewhere farther inside. items.body: I am sitting in the darkStaring at nothingCaged by the shadows I become rottenMy emotions go to another stageEscape from this cave Plato’s allegory of the cave begins with one of philosophy’s most unsettling propositions: human beings may spend their lives confusing appearances for reality. His prisoners, chained underground since childhood, know the world through forms projected across stone. To encounter the world beyond their enclosure would require a painful revision of everything they believed to be true. Knowledge, in this conception, begins with the terrifying possibility that the mind has mistaken confinement for the universe. Berlin-based Brazilian artist Daniel Knutz brings that ancient problem inward on The Cave, turning Plato’s cavern into an enclosure built from memory, fear, exhaustion, and emotional paralysis. The walls possess their own acoustics. Thoughts return altered by repetition; tears strike stone; a heartbeat seems to travel through chambers where time has become difficult to measure. Knutz presents consciousness as something almost geological, with experience deposited layer upon layer until the past acquires the weight of rock. Musically, The Cave belongs to the grander tradition of darkwave and gothic rock represented by Clan of Xymox, Fields of the Nephilim, Danse Society, and London After Midnight. There is breadth in its atmosphere and a sense of scale suited to Knutz’s subject. The production treats space as an instrument: distant sounds, cavernous resonance, and deliberate repetition make the listener aware of imagined dimensions beyond the speakers. It feels less like observing someone’s isolation than occupying its architecture. Memory is rarely an archive from which we retrieve pristine records. Each recollection passes once more through the mind that remembers it, altered by present fear, desire, guilt, and age. Knutz’s cave therefore becomes an enormous resonating chamber in which consciousness continually encounters itself. “The Cave is a journey into the depths of my own mind,” says Knutz. “The cave symbolizes the hidden places within us where memories echo, fears grow, and emotions remain trapped in darkness. The atmosphere of the song is shaped by the sounds of the cave itself: distant echoes, dripping water, and tears falling onto stone. These sounds represent memories and emotions repeating through time, creating a feeling of isolation and reflection. Even the heartbeat feels as if it is resonating through the cold walls, emphasizing the loneliness and weight of the moment.” The accompanying video, conceived and directed by Streykatt, extends this idea into mountains and an underground cavern rendered in drained, earthen tones. Knutz moves through terrain that seems older than individual suffering, reducing one person’s crisis against the immense scale of stone and geological time. The imagery gives his solitude a strange, almost prehistoric quality. Watch the video for The Cave below: Yet Plato’s prisoners were offered the possibility of ascent. Daniel Knutz leaves that possibility painfully open: self-knowledge as illumination is earned through confrontation, when the mind finally recognizes the walls surrounding it. Somewhere beyond the cold stone, another conception of the self remains possible. The first evidence of freedom may simply be realizing that the cave has an exit. The cave is included on Daniel Knutz’s latest album, Echoes. Listen to The Cave below and order the album here. items.body: There are places on Earth that seem to contain more world than geography should permit. A shoreline at dusk, an abandoned road, a drowned foundation beneath still water: each can suggest that reality possesses hidden rooms, inaccessible except through attention. On Illusion of an Inland Ocean, due October 30, Eric Angelo Bessel makes music for that suspicion, eighteen connected compositions in which ordinary terrain seems to open upon immensities. Based in Portland, Oregon, Bessel works at the intersection of memory, landscape, and technology, subjects united by their peculiar relationship with time. His music, photography, and design all share an interest in the traces people and places leave behind: evidence that something existed, changed, disappeared, or continues beyond immediate perception. Across his various disciplines, he seems less interested in documenting the world as it appears than in examining how perception alters it, and how memory can transform a place into something larger, stranger, and almost limitless. The first single, Pathways, released on August 25, offers an ideal entry point. Its patient, ambient movement recalls The Caretaker, William Basinski, Loscil, Stars of the Lid, and Faten Kanaan, yet Bessel approaches that lineage with a distinct sense of terrestrial mystery. The music feels cinematic and powerful because it enlarges perception. A familiar landscape begins to seem ancient; a road becomes a coordinate; water becomes an archive. Tiny details acquire the gravity of astronomical objects viewed from a distance. Mellotrons, guitars, and layers of analogue processing become instruments of gradual revelation, with tones accumulating, dissolving, and returning in altered forms. Melody seems to come into focus by degrees, as though perceived across a great distance, while small shifts in texture can change the apparent dimensions of the entire piece. The music encourages sustained attention rather than movement toward some final point, rewarding repeated listening with connections that may have remained invisible before. Its accompanying visualizer deepens that sensation by placing us underwater, where life passes through channels of static and unstable transmission. The images suggest cameras lowered into a region beyond human access, recording organisms, currents, and possible thresholds that our senses were never designed to comprehend. The ocean has always possessed this cosmic quality. We know its presence intimately, yet portions of it remain unseen, populated by forms of life so remote from daily experience that they can seem almost extraterrestrial. Watch the video for Pathways below: Written, recorded, mixed, and produced entirely by Bessel, Illusion of an Inland Ocean is expansive without becoming crowded. Tones gather slowly, suspended in spaces, while distant textures seem to recede beyond the edge of hearing. There is a frequency of peace running through the record, though serenity here is never simple. Silence becomes evidence, a faint indication that something vast continues beyond the narrow bandwidth of human awareness. Beneath it lies the awareness that the universe, and even our planet, remains filled with regions we cannot completely know. Composed in the pale hours of early morning and refined deep into the night, the album occupies that uncertain territory where dreams, memory, and observation begin to lose their boundaries. Bessel has long been drawn to these transitional states, when the mind has loosened its allegiance to ordinary time and the familiar world can suddenly appear immense, remote, or newly discovered. Bessel treats mystery as a condition of existence rather than a puzzle awaiting solution. The album asks for stillness, the kind that precedes sleep, when the architecture of the waking world loosens and distances become difficult to measure. Listening then can feel like drifting beyond the mapped edge of experience, not toward fantasy so much as toward a heightened awareness of how little we perceive. In that sense, Bessel has made an album about scale: the immense concealed inside the commonplace, the unknown beneath our feet, and the quiet possibility that every familiar place contains a portal to somewhere we have never been. items.body: A few years ago, the International Anthem label was pretty much the hottest shit in the improvised music genre. Irreversible Entanglements, the late Jaimie Branch, Ben LaMar Gay, Angel Bat Dawid, Makaya McCraven, Jeff Parker, Damon Locks - they had them all. Lately, though, the focus seemed to have shifted more towards world music and alternative stuff. That’s where SML’s new album comes in at just the right time to set the record straight a bit. SML is an International Anthem in-house supergroup consisting of Josh Johnson (saxophones), Gregory Uhlmann (guitar), Jeremiah Chiu (synthesizer, electronics), Anna Butterss (bass) and Booker Stardrum (drums), which has released two studio albums to date - Small Medium Large (2024) (which could also be read as a moniker for SML) and How You Been (2025). The hallmarks of their music can already be found on these two albums: repetitive structures, subtle shifts in the architecture of the pieces, and an affinity for deliberate monotony and world music. However, the term “studio album” isn’t entirely accurate, since How You Been , for example, consists of performances from the Empty Bottle in Chicago, the Tractor Tavern in Seattle, and the Zebulon in Los Angeles, which were condensed into three- and four-minute highlights. What might sound somewhat dismissive here are, in fact, moments of immense concentration and intensity, distilled from a continuous stream of consciousness and an almost magical band chemistry. The reason is simple: SML are a live band. And the references to their musical influences are obvious: 1970s Miles Davis, the Sun Ra Arkestra, Neu!, King Crimson and Can. You can really feel this in the way the band tries to make the pull of their music physically palpable during live performances. They create a form of ecstatic minimalism by stretching individual motifs to the point of trance. Spontaneous Music Live was once again recorded in front of a live audience at Zebulon in Los Angeles. What sets it apart from its predecessors is the immediacy of the recording and the near-total absence of post-production. The album consists of two long tracks, each over twenty minutes in length, and demonstrates what SML is capable of when their music isn’t forced into the confines of a standard song length. The result of these session-style improvisations reveals great discipline, dynamics, and a distinct artistic vision. Take “Roundabouts (Live)”, for example, the B-side of the LP. It starts with a delicate saxophone melody, metronome-like drumming and a concise synthesizer riff, which eventually spiral completely out of control. What Spontaneous Music Live succeeds in doing - unlike its two predecessor albums - is to bring the psychedelic nature of the music into sharp focus. It’s easy to imagine the band playing at the big festivals of the late 1960s - the hippies would have loved their style and sound. Actually, it’s music to “turn on, tune in, and drop out“, except that you don’t need drugs to enjoy it - the music itself is the drug. SML are trippy in the best possible way. Spontaneous Music Live is available on vinyl, cassette and as a download. You can listen to it and buy it here: Spontaneous Music Live by SML Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
The Brief Guide To Ākāśa Gathering

26 August 2026

Making its debut on September 4-6, Ākāśa Gathering will unfold 3,500 metres up in the high desert of Ladakh, on a terraced hillside site in Karu, a village roughly 35-45 minutes from Leh town. Named for the Sanskrit word for sky, the three-day, three-night gathering is a first edition that aims to create an intimate gathering with "fewer people, lighter footprint, deeper listening" and an ethos of "leave-no-trace".

Music

Indian live acts like Komorebi, Anhad + Tanner and Curtain Blue will play alongside ambient, noise and experimental acts including Fursat FM and Qareebi, as well as genre-spanning DJs like Kaleekarma, Sheral, and Nida in a B2B with Discokid. Techno acts of the country will also be represented through a live set by Monophonik and B2B sets between Kohra and Norway's Marius Bø, Dotdat and Berlin's Chloe Lula, AAGUU and Brooklyn's DJ Voices. Other international acts on the lineup include Japan's house-techno force Gonno, Berlin's Sol Asylum Records label-head Julie Marghilano, and Germany's Fejka. Special highlights include Mumbai's Sickflip revitalising his early-career work 'The Ladakh Project' more than a decade after its release, traditional Persian instrument player and regular electronica collaborator Mohammad Reza Mortazavi bringing his meteoric rise to the country and a performance by Indian leftfield artist Ruhail Qaisar who performs in the very home region that he centred for his lauded work 'Fatima'.

Wellness

The Indus, named for the river that's shaped Ladakh for centuries, is the festival's dedicated wellness space, holding the hours between sets with breath, movement and stillness at altitude. It brings Mihir Jogh for Gather & Ground and Mini Shastri for Slow Strong Mornings & Evenings. Gillian and Grey of Lotus Beings lead Yin Yoga and Grounding Tai Chi, and Martin Dubois & Ashwini with a Musical Nap session.

Workshops & Experiences

Between the mornings and the music, the festival's workshops and experiences programme runs on craft, food and conversation drawn from the region: cyanotype printing and toning with Parkhang Collective, a Kashmiri Naqashi workshop, natural dyeing and weaving with Lena Ladakh, a Lune Book Club sitting, stargazing with Dark Sky, and a walk along the Indus with Knowhere Travels.

Tickets to Ākāśa Gathering are on sale via District, and more information is available on the festival's website.

items.body:
Since everyone else has written something about the centennials of Miles Davis and John Coltrane, why not join the parade? It is a good opportunity to look at the timeline of bassists the legendary trumpeter and saxophonist used. Born just under four months apart, the pair worked together under the elder Davis’ name periodically between Fall 1955 and Spring 1957 before a more steady affiliation in 1958-1960.

It is in that latter period that this analysis will begin, as it gives a convenient bit of serendipity: the fact that two of the their most famed albums were made in that period, Davis’ Kind Blue (March 2nd and April 22nd, 1959 for Columbia) and Coltrane’s Giant Steps (May 4th–5th and December 2nd, 1959). And the analysis will end with Coltrane’s death in 1967, which came during the tenure of Davis’ “second great quintet” and before his groups swelled and electrified during his fusion period.

As such, we begin with the same man, the bassist on both those albums: Paul Chambers. He had taken up the bass a decade earlier in his adopted home of Detroit (where he was a student at the seminal Cass Technical High School ... more on that later). He arrived in New York in 1954 at 19. By the time of Kind of Blue and Giant Steps, he had been on over 100 sessions from dozens of leaders, with multiple dates under Davis (with whom he had started working in late 1955) and Coltrane (who had used him for several albums in 1957-58 as well as both fellow sideman for many others and Chambers also hiring Coltrane for his own sessions). In addition to the five albums he led, Chambers played on sessions for Benny Golson, Curtis Fuller, J.J. Johnson, Lee Morgan, Red Garland, Sonny Clark, and Sonny Rollins.

The collaboration between Davis and Chambers was remarkably fruitful before and after Kind of Blue and solidified a part of Davis’ music that had previously seen widely differing players like Tommy Potter, Oscar Pettiford, Al McKibbon, and Percy Heath. The rest of 1959 saw multiple engagements around the country and closed with recordings that would be part of another monumental record, Sketches of Spain, that paired Davis’ group with the Gil Evans Orchestra. 1960 continued that momentum with more Sketches of Spain recording and almost non-stop touring, including two stretches in Europe, from Spring onward. 1961 and 1962 had more of the same activity, the documents being Someday My Prince Will Come and Quiet Nights. Then, quite suddenly, Chambers left Davis’ group in early February 1963.

It should be stated that Chambers did not restrict his activities solely to Davis, recording over four dozen albums during the period with, among many others, Jackie McLean, Wynton Kelly, Benny Golson, Hank Mobley, and Curtis Fuller. And after leaving Davis, he worked steadily with an array of leaders through the end of 1968, sadly passing away from tuberculosis caused and/or aggravated by drug abuse at only 33.

Stepping right into the Davis group was another Cass Technical High School alumnus: Ron Carter. Nearly 26, Carter was already prophesying his prolific career, participating in over three dozen albums since 1960, with the likes of Charli Persip, Yusef Lateef, Eric Dolphy, Don Ellis, Coleman Hawkins, Cecil Payne, Jaki Byard, Wes Montgomery, Bobby Timmons, Tadd Dameron, Dizzy Reece, Ken McIntyre, Milt Jackson, Benny Golson and others, plus waxing his leader debut, Where?, for Prestige subsidiary New Jazz in 1961.

It was Carter’s arrival that heralded Davis’ soon-to-be seminal band, though it took until Fall 1964 for its personnel to solidify. With Carter, Davis recorded Seven Steps To Heaven and played the Antibes festival in 1963. What is interesting though is while the “second great quintet” is thought of as a monolith, the bass chair had some upheaval/fluidity, depending on how you look at it. Gary Peacock – already a veteran and likely the only person to work for both Bud Shank and Albert Ayler – took the chair for nearly six weeks in the spring of 1964, Carter returning thereafter through the end of the year. 1965 began auspiciously with the January recording of E.S.P. but then things derailed with a convalescing Davis unable to play. And when he could, in November and December, Carter, a hot commodity, was absent, spelled by Peacock once more, then Reggie Workman, who had come up around the same time as Carter and had already come and gone in the groups of Coltrane. In 1966, Carter would return to the group but only partially, participating in East Coast performances, shows elsewhere having either Richard Davis, Carter’s only real equal in terms of fecundity, or in the Peacock mold of eclecticism, Eddie Gomez, returning permanently in October, just before the album Miles Smiles. 1967 was similar: Carter was on board when not busy elsewhere, Gomez on call, then Albert Stinson for one show (a little over two years before his passing – see Bass Tragedies column in Issue 94) and then another veteran, Buster Williams, for a tour (and playing on one track of the 1981-released compilation album Directions). Carter would fill a fixed point for all of 1967, including the albums Sorcerer and Nefertiti and would continue with Davis through the middle of 1968.

Like Chambers or perhaps even more so, Carter was also on the greater jazz scene during his tenure with Davis. He recorded on sessions led by his fellow Davis bandmates but also by everyone from Bobby Timmons, Charles Lloyd, Donald Byrd and Bobby Hutcherson to Jimmy Smith, Shirley Scott, Eddie Harris, and Stanley Turrentine, to name only a handful. He has, of course, gone on to be likely the most recorded bassist in jazz history.

Paul Chambers’ time under Coltrane was shorter and more intermittent. After Giant Steps he was part of, along with the rest of Davis’ period band, November 1959 recordings that would partly comprise Coltrane Jazz and be brought back 18 months later as one of three individual bassists taking part in the Africa/Brass recordings (though his contribution was only heard on the 1995 complete sessions version).

Also in 1959 was a Birdland engagement for Coltrane where either Ahmed Abdul-Malik or George Tucker, both established and close in age to Coltrane, were on bass.

In 1960 Coltrane hired the slightly younger Steve Davis in what seems to be his first professional engagement. Davis stayed in the band through the end of the year for all its live dates and played on music recorded in October and released piecemeal on My Favorite Things, Coltrane Jazz, Coltrane Plays the Blues, and Coltrane’s Sound. Though Davis lived until 1987, his credits after Coltrane were slight: the Mangione Brothers, Dave Burns, McCoy Tyner, Kenny Dorham, James Moody, Freddie McCoy, and Eddie Jefferson, all made in the ‘60s. One deviation in the year came via Coltrane’s shared date with Don Cherry, The Avant-Garde, where bass was handled by either Charlie Haden or Percy Heath.

1961 was a year in flux, bassist-wise, for Coltrane. He introduced a concept to which he would return later in the decade by using two bassists for an engagement at Chicago’s Sutherland Lounge in March: Raphael Don Garrett and Workman, the former, about six years younger, working with Roland Kirk, Paul Serrano, and Eddie Harris, the latter 11 years younger, sideman for Gigi Gryce, Donald Byrd, Duke Jordan, Richard Williams, and Dave Pike.

Workman would be part of the aforementioned Africa/Brass, as would, separately, another bassist, Art Davis, already with credits under Max Roach, Lee Morgan, Booker Little, Hal Mooney, Ernestine Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie, Leo Wright, Clifford Jordan/Sonny Red, Abbey Lincoln, and Booker Little. But in May they were together for Ole Coltrane and nearly a month at the Village Vanguard in August. Workman would become the fixed bassist for Coltrane through the end of the year for concerts, including a European tour, and a small portion of the Ballads album from the end of the year. An exception was Workman either alternating or alongside Jimmy Garrison for a November stint at the Village Vanguard.

If not for a family health crisis forcing Workman to leave the group at the end of 1961 and return to his native Philadelphia, he likely would have stayed with the band and jazz history been quite different. It should be said that Workman hardly is a footnote, becoming one of the most revered players of his generation. But it was Garrison who became the anchor. Born between Garrett and Workman, prior to joining Coltrane he had worked with Philly Joe Jones, Curtis Fuller, Kenny Dorham, Jackie McLean, JR Montrose, Walter Bishop, Jr., Ornette Coleman, Bill Barron, and Ted Curson.

Unlike Carter and Davis, once Garrison was on board, he stayed there. That was mostly to do with Coltrane’s packed schedule of touring and albums and that, unlike Davis, he was healthy and non-combustible. From 1962-1964, Garrison was omnipresent, including the bulk of Ballads, Duke Ellington & John Coltrane (where he split duties with Ellington’s period bassist Aaron Bell), 2018 discovery Both Directions At Once, John Coltrane And Johnny Hartman, Impressions, Crescent, another new millennium unearthed gem in Blue World, and closing out the year with Coltrane’s magnum opus A Love Supreme (which added Art Davis for a second day of recording, released as a second disc to the album’s deluxe edition in 2002).

In 1965 Garrison was still the main man but occasionally Davis would be alongside him: partially on The John Coltrane Quartet Plays in February and fully for June’s Ascension. Otherwise, Garrison was the sole bassist for performances and most of the other albums: Transition, Sun Ship, and Meditations. The exceptions without Davis were overdubs of Haden for the posthumously released Infinity and Garrett returning to play both bass and clarinet for Live In Seattle (as well as the 2021 archival release A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle), Om, and part of Kulu Se Mama.

1966 was even more Garrison-centric, with the only documented work including a second bassist shows in November and December with Lionel “Sonny” Johnson, the brother of Dewey Johnson, who had played on Ascension. The last year of Coltrane’s life, Garrison was there as well, with one notable absence: the Coltrane/Rashied Ali duet Interstellar Space.

Unlike Chambers or Carter, Garrison was kept so busy during his time with Coltrane that his outside discography at the time is meager, though it does include his sole leader date, Illumination! with the Elvin Jones/Jimmy Garrison Sextet. Otherwise it was sessions with Lorez Alexandria, Coltrane bandmate McCoy Tyner, Sonny Rollins, Bill Dixon, and Robert F. Pozar.

After Coltrane’s death, Garrison kept working but his documentation slowed, his two Blue Note dates with the Jones trio rounded out by Joe Farrell being the most enduring. There were also dates with Rolf and Joachim Kuhn, Clifford Thornton and Nathan Davis, and regular work with Alice Coltrane and Archie Shepp. His final recording came in early 1975 with Beaver Harris and Dave Burrell’s 360 Degree Music Experience. Garrison died of lung cancer in 1976 at 42.

items.body:
1970 (April 10th, 1970 – IBC Studios, London)

Negotiations were now underway between Sean Murphy and several labels including Deram, CBS and Harvest, the EMI sub-label that had distributed Volume Two in the UK and already had Kevin Ayers in its stable. “They are still not an attraction in the very top bracket, so it was a pleasant surprise to see major companies throwing in genuinely massive bids earlier this year when the group was looking for a recording deal,” Richard Williams revealed. Ultimately, Soft Machine signed with CBS, but Third was self-financed, taken partly from studio sessions, but also from live recordings (“Facelift”) and edits and loops of tapes made by Mike Ratledge and Hugh Hopper at the home of Bob Woolford, who had let them use his Brenell and Stellavox tape recorders. Such infringements of accepted professional practices were only possible because CBS, having acquired a finished album, were no longer in a position to force the band to comply with them.

The benefit for Soft Machine in terms of artistic freedom is easy to measure. But this has to be balanced against the fact that the production on Third is, to put it bluntly, an unmitigated disaster. IBC, at the time the studio of choice for such notorious perfectionists as The Who and the Bee Gees, are probably less to blame than the band themselves who, in spite of the issues with Volume Two, are again credited as sole producers. The sound suffers from almost constantly saturated low frequencies and extremely vague mediums, the drums are much too low in the mix, as if played behind a closed door; and the organ is deprived of much of its biting impact through overwhelming equalization. Unfortunately the 2007 remaster, while an improvement, fails to rectify this.

What is problematic is that, as well as making the album an uncomfortable listen, its sub-par production lessens the claim, widely held at the time of its release, that Third represented musical state-of-the-art. This claim was based on Soft Machine’s ability, unparalleled among their contemporaries, to draw from and amalgamate an exceptionally wide range of influences. Starting out as a rock band, and then gradually moving towards jazz to invent a uniquely personal, and absolutely valid, British answer to American fusion, Soft Machine went even further, incorporating the influence of Stockhausen’s avant-garde and Terry Riley’s repetitive minimalism. Third’s ‘total’ vision, encompassing the entire spectrum of known musical genres, placed Soft Machine at the forefront of musical “progress” in 1970. However, horizons have since expanded to such an extent, beyond the Western tradition in particular, that this concept of universality has aged considerably.

In his insightful review of Third for Actuel, Paul Alessandrini wrote of “music to really listen to, no longer aiming for a purely physical vibration, more interiorized. Soft Machine have re-thought their musical influences – Riley, Cecil Taylor, Coltrane – to really make them their own, abandoning their aesthetics of random explosion in favor of a much more thought-out approach.” There are still occasional reminders of these sonic excesses that, as Alessandrini noted, had now largely disappeared from their music. Mike Ratledge's lengthy solo introduction to “Facelift” almost sounds like an electric exorcism, as if to rid Soft Machine of what still remains of that violence in order to reinvent their music in a more controlled manner, setting formal perfection as their new objective.

Considered as a whole, Hugh Hopper's piece represents the last remnant of Soft Machine’s early days, when they still favored spirit over form - here found lacking in both sound quality and performance, with a few train wrecks along the way - and were intent on disregarding the accepted rules. “Facelift” includes free sections increasingly at odds with Ratledge’s preoccupation with structure – and while as a keyboard player, he still embodies the band’s more radical leanings, Ratledge’s own compositions reveal a much less iconoclastic temperament. Hopper described his own approach at the time as “halfway between” that of Dean, “whose thing is really total improvisation, without any structure, and on the other extreme, [that of Ratledge] who's into entirely formalized musical forms.

“Moon in June” completes Robert Wyatt’s donation to Soft Machine of the material originally intended for his first solo album in 1968. It is interesting to note that Wyatt does this at the exact point where Soft Machine had shed any remaining reference to pop in their live repertoire. Looking back, Wyatt was certainly justified in saying that his side of Third was “the last chance I had to use all the things we'd done without being a jazz band. I wanted to get twenty minutes of it down somewhere.” And since his colleagues, reluctant to act as mere accompanists, had made no secret of their lack of interest in his songs, he recorded most of “Moon in June” on his own, repeating the modus operandi of the 1968-69 demo. Hugh Hopper and Mike Ratledge’s participation is again limited to the organ solo halfway through (Hopper also plays a short melodic theme earlier in the piece). Elton Dean wasn’t asked to contribute anything – Wyatt’s unconvincing justification being that he “hadn’t yet worked out how to work on [his] stuff with the added wind instruments.”

As there was no mention of this breach of band discipline in the sleeve notes, only the most astute listeners noticed that the organ heard during the first ten minutes was a Hammond rather than Ratledge’s signature Lowrey, that the playing clearly wasn’t Ratledge’s, and that most of the ‘bass’ parts were played on an electric piano. When the truth was finally revealed, Wyatt gave contradictory versions of what had happened – in one interview claiming that Ratledge and Hopper had “refused to play [on “Moon in June”] and I had to play it all myself,” in another that he’d “almost had to force them to get them to play on it, which I thought was rather unfair as I’d done my best to get into the music they were writing.” Probably the most objective and believable of Wyatt’s rationales was that he was “terrified it’d be played wrong” if he didn’t perform it all himself.

To approach “Moon in June” as a ‘message’ song would misrepresent Wyatt’s more mundane intent, insofar as the phonetic qualities of the words often seem to matter more to him than their meaning. In other words, “Moon in June” is above all a musical composition, a suite of instrumental sections, some of which are adorned with melodies and lyrics, and others not. The singing accompanies the music rather than vice-versa. In this respect, outside of a possible rivalry with Elton Dean and Wyatt’s inability to sing while drumming, there was no theoretical incompatibility between Soft Machine’s move towards jazz and the continued presence of Wyatt’s voice (even if limited to the Echoplexed scat singing of his solitary interludes during the band’s concerts). Dispensing with vocals was the single most questionable move in Soft Machine’s entire musical evolution, not to mention one whose commercial consequences cannot be underestimated. In different circumstances, Hugh Hopper would surely have joined Wyatt in lobbying for having at least some vocals, but in addition to his increasingly strained personal relationship with Wyatt, Hopper had at this point completely lost interest in non-instrumental music. “I find that using the human voice means asserting limitations to your music right from the start”, he explained in 1972. “I am more interested in the sounds generated by instruments, or electronic devices, because the possibilities offered by songs are much more limited than when experimenting with sounds.”

Even if there was no future for singing in Soft Machine, “Moon in June” at least offers evidence that Robert Wyatt, in a voice-free context, could still be more than “a session drummer for an interesting new species of jazz groups,” as long as he contributed to the writing. When it came to extended pieces, he could stand comparison with Mike Ratledge, even though he lacked any comparable academic background. In addition to its constant melodic inspiration, “Moon in June” is very skillfully constructed (indeed, its instrumental architecture had remained intact since 1968), and confirms Wyatt’s seemingly innate talent for making a coherent whole out of ill-assorted musical ideas.

items._cn_summary: Soft Machine的《Third》是坎特伯雷场景的代表作，融合摇滚、爵士、斯托克豪森式先锋派与莱利式极简主义，试图以全景式视角囊括已知音乐类型。专辑在录音室与现场录音基础上，通过磁带编辑与循环手法拼贴完成，展现了乐队对声音结构的实验性处理。然而乐评指出其制作存在严重问题，低频饱和、中频模糊、鼓组音量过低，限制了作品原本应达到的听觉说服力，也削弱了其作为1970年前沿音乐代表的普遍性主张。尽管2007年重制有所改善，仍未能完全修复。整体上，这是一张在艺术野心与客观技术条件之间形成张力的前卫融合专辑，其历史价值与听觉体验存在落差。

items.body: Sonic Pieces are releasing two special records in November. The latest release in their Patterns Series is a collaboration between Oliver Doerell and Jawad Salkhordeh, and mixes Eastern mysticism with Western electronics. The alteration of its tones are mixed in with segments of inserted voice, while distortions and lacerations scar the music’s surface. With Persian influences and light, jazz-oriented vibes, complete with its pungent cigarette smoke which loiters well beyond midnight, occupies its own unique zone in electro-acoustic instrumental music. The soundscapes have no particular home and defy genre-categorisation, which is perfect, as music shouldn’t be limited to boxed-in styles or conventions. It finds its home in the unknown, unexplored areas of sound, in the liberal, sprawling paths within; areas not yet mapped out. Spellbinding rhythms slip into the fabric of its sound with ease, and the music seems to be well-balanced. The second release from Sonic Pieces sees the completion of Otto A Totland’s piano trilogy. Named Companion, the sparse piano compositions are a distillation of purity. Totland has further refined his craft, and the music that emerges is heartfelt. Sparse does not have to mean skeletal, cold, or stark, and Companion is a prime example of that. Warmth flows like a heart pumping blood through the arteries, with every note occupying a special place and providing critical links to the main body of the song. The music is personal to Otto, so much so that the piano becomes an extension of himself. Companion is warmth in a cruel world, like a genuine smile in a world of fakery and falsehood, a true friend amid backstabbing and infighting. A diamond in the rough. Obscured by daily tragedies which continue to litter the news, music such as this is comfort food. Glints of peace and a lambent hope emerge thanks to the knowledge that rays of goodness, decency, and purity still exist…if you know where to look. www.sonicpieces.com
items._genre: experimental / electro-acoustic / electronic / world fusion / contemporary classical / jazz
items._cn_summary: 该乐评聚焦Sonic Pieces厂牌十一月发行的两张唱片。其一为Oliver Doerell与Jawad Salkhordeh在Patterns系列中的合作，将东方神秘主义与西方电子声响交织，融入波斯音乐气息与轻爵士氛围，人声片段、失真和撕裂痕迹附着于音乐表面，形成难以归类的电声原声器乐景观。其二为Otto A Totland钢琴三部曲的完结篇《Companion》，以稀疏钢琴独奏呈现，但音符之间充满温度与内在联结，钢琴仿若演奏者自身的延伸。两张作品均跨越类型界限，在实验、电子、世界音乐与当代古典的交叉地带找到平衡，既保留了声响的探索性，又赋予作品以真诚的情感内核。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music.
